_note: Engine-level constants the design handoff did not specify. Kept out of the design's own JSON files so those stay exactly as delivered. Still content, not code — CLAUDE.md forbids balance constants living in source.

combat._hitClipNote: How long the recoil clip plays, and how hurt an enemy has to be before it switches to its injured walk. Both are RENDER-ONLY -- neither changes damage, speed or any decision the sim makes, so tuning them cannot move balance. `injuredBelowPct` is a percentage of max hp; a sheet with no `walkHurt` clip simply keeps walking normally, which is what makes it safe to ship before every animal has the art.
combat._hitFlashNote: The flash is 60ms as the spec asks, but 60ms only reads as a blink if it is allowed to end. It was re-armed on every hit INCLUDING damage-over-time ticks, so at late-wave fire rates it never expired: wave 15 with 266 enemies rendered most of the crowd as solid white silhouettes and the wave-12 boss could not be seen at all while being fought. DoT no longer flashes, and the refractory caps the duty cycle at 60/(60+160) = 27%, so a hit reads as a blink against the sprite rather than replacing it. Raise the refractory if a crowd still washes out; lower it if single hits stop registering.

camera._zoomNote: Zoom is derived, not fixed: round(canvasHeight / targetWorldHeight), integer only, clamped. A fixed zoom made screen size and DPI control HOW MUCH WORLD you see - at 1920x1080 dpr 1.5 the view was 810 world px tall, so the farmer was 2% of screen width and every round a speck. 560 lands on ~540 world px on every screen from 1080p to 4K, which is the SAME view a 1080p dpr-1 screen always had: the framing that was already right, now independent of monitor and DPI. It is deliberately NOT tighter - the rounds were made legible by packing bigger art, not by cropping the field, and cropping costs you the warning time to see a horde coming. Small screens bottom out at minZoom and show less; that is the integer-zoom floor, not a target.

fx._note: Conformed FX clips (art/sprites.json -> fx). `life` is how long the whole clip plays, in seconds — the renderer divides it by the clip's packed frame count, so retiming an effect is this number and nothing else. Effects are decoration: when the pool is full the sim drops them silently rather than perturbing a seeded run.
fx._rates: Hit sparks on every hit would be 200 sparks a frame in a late wave and would bury the enemies. `hitSparkChance` is the fraction of non-crit hits that spark; crits always do, because a crit is the thing you want to notice.
fx._recoil: How long a weapon's firing kick lasts and how far it travels. The ring these once belonged to is gone (see `carry` below); the kick survived it, because a kick is what makes a weapon read as FIRING rather than as an icon that happens to be there.
fx._newClips: Clips from the unTied projectile packs. shockwave replaces the conformed FX-pack ring for ground pulses; arrowImpact and bigImpact are the dedicated impact animations those packs ship, which the FX pack had no equivalent of.
fx._jabNote: The pitchfork's attack, and the only melee presentation in the game that is not a sweep. It used to draw a white crescent (`fx.slash`) over `proj.claw` — which is `pj3_demon_bite_loop_large_orange`, a DEMON BITE, stretched to the swing's 78px diameter. The owner called it a giant sand mouth eating things, and it was: a sword's swing and a monster's bite on a tool that stabs. What replaces it is three things and no atlas art at all. The held fork lunges (`carryThrustPixels` on the weapon, `thrustSeconds` below), three short strokes fly out at the tine tips, and a spark lands where a tine does. Stroked lines rather than a generated clip because a clip at this size is a smudge and a line is a line — tried at 1x in a real run, which is the only scale that settles it. Nothing here is in the sim: the hitbox, its radius, its arc and its cooldown are exactly what they were, and a fixed seed reports the same numbers either side.
fx._harvestToolNote: The pickaxe and axe hanging at the player's feet are not weapons and are not part of the carried loadout — see `Renderer.collectHarvestTools`. This is the flat multiplier they draw at; it used to be `weaponRingScale * 0.85` and is now written out, because the ring it borrowed from no longer exists.

playerMark._note: The mark under the player's feet, and the only thing on the field that is his alone. Enemy humanoids share his rig, and repainting the farmhand fixed his CLOTHES without giving the eye anything positive to lock onto in a crowd -- so this is the other half: a soft contact shadow with a faint lamp ring around it, drawn once per frame in the ground layer under every sprite, exactly where the dash dust goes. Nothing else in the game draws one, so it never needs to compete.
playerMark._restraintNote: This is a farm at dusk, not a MOBA. The numbers below are deliberately near the bottom of what still reads: the shadow does most of the work by GROUNDING him, the ring only has to survive a squint. Raise ringAlpha before raising ringWidth -- a thick ring reads as UI drawn over the world, a faint wide one reads as lamplight on grass. If it ever starts to look like a selection circle it has gone too far.
playerMark._footNote: NEGATIVE, and measured, not assumed: the character sheets are 32x64 cells drawn from bottom-centre, but the art stands with its feet at cell row 52 -- twelve pixels ABOVE the cell floor (tools/pixellab-cut.ts, and the LimeZu farmer sheets share the baseline). The player origin is therefore the cell floor, not his boots, and an ellipse drawn there reads as a hole he is hovering over; the owner saw exactly that. -10 puts it on the boot row with the couple of pixels of bias that stops it striping the boots.

carry._note: Where a weapon sits ON THE BODY. This replaces the weapon ring — six icons at 15px on a perfect circle, which read as an orbit and told you nothing about how armed the farmhand was. A carried loadout is the same information drawn as equipment: the thing that just fired is in his hands, everything else hangs off him at roughly life scale, and its per-tier art means a merged weapon visibly becomes a better object.
carry._anchorNote: `dx`/`dy` are the anchor for a slot, in world pixels, PER FACING, and `dy` is measured from the BOOTS (negative is up) rather than from the player origin — the origin is the character cell's floor, twelve pixels under his feet, and every anchor here would otherwise carry that twelve around with it. `bootOffsetY` is the one place that conversion lives. See playerMark._footNote for where the measurement comes from. For scale: the drawn farmhand is 52px tall and 30px wide in front view and about 20px wide in profile, so his hips are about -20, his shoulders about -38 and the top of his hat about -50. The slots are a LADDER and nothing shares a rung -- hips -18, hand -23, backX -29, back -35, shoulder -37 -- because in profile he is only twenty pixels wide and anchors on the same rung all land on the same twenty pixels. That is what put three weapons on his chin the first time.
carry._behindNote: `behind` says whether this slot draws BEHIND the character for that facing, and it is the whole of the depth handling: carried items are pushed at the player's own y, and the sprite pass is a counting sort that preserves insertion order inside a bucket, so `behind` items are simply pushed before the player sprite and the rest after. A rifle slung on his back is behind him when he faces the camera and in front of him when he walks away, which is what stops the loadout reading as decals stuck on top of him. Use it sparingly: an item drawn behind a 30px-wide body is mostly an item you cannot see, which is why the back slots sit off-centre.
carry._flipNote: `flip` mirrors the art horizontally for that facing. All the source art points right, so the left-facing views need it. `angle` is the resting rotation in radians, clockwise, and a weapon's own `carryAngle` in weapons.json is ADDED to it.
carry._thrustNote: How long the held-weapon LUNGE lasts, for weapons that declare `carryThrustPixels`. Read off `slot.firedAt`, the world-tick stamp the sim already writes to decide which weapon is in his hands — so the thrust is derived from state that exists, adds none, and cannot move an outcome. The curve is a half sine: out and back, peak at the halfway mark. Kept slightly longer than `weaponRecoilSeconds` (0.12) on purpose — a gun's kick should be over before you see it and a thrust should not.
carry._muzzleNote: The muzzle flash leaves the END OF THE HELD WEAPON now, not a fixed sixteen pixels along the way the man happens to be walking -- which put the flash behind him whenever he fired at something he was not facing, which for an auto-targeting weapon is most of the time. It is derived, not authored: the `hand` anchor for his class and facing gives the grip, and the muzzle is `1 - carryPivot` of the weapon's `carryHeight` forward along its AIM. `muzzleReachFallback` is the old sixteen, kept for anything that fires without carried art so nothing regressed on the way in. Decoration only: `playFx` draws no random numbers, so this cannot move the sim's RNG stream and a seed still replays.
carry._orderNote: The slot a weapon asks for is its RESTING slot; `hand` is dynamic and belongs to whichever weapon fired most recently (`slot.firedAt`, a sim tick stamp). Everything else claims its declared slot in pickup order, and a weapon that finds its slot taken walks forward through this cycle, wrapping, until it finds a free one. `hand` is struck out of the free set first, so a resting weapon never lands in it. Six inventory slots against `hand` plus five anchors means the loadout always fits exactly, with no overflow case to invent.
carry._twoFamiliesNote: The rest angles look arbitrary until you notice the atlas holds TWO families pointing two ways. `gun.*` and `carry.*` are side views pointing RIGHT; `weapon.*` is a 3/4 tool icon standing UP. So the hips' 1.15 radians hangs a gun down the thigh, which is what it was tuned for, and swings a pitchfork out sideways past the width of the man. Lowering it to 0.6 was tried and is exactly backwards -- it stands the pitchfork up and lays the guns out flat, which is worse, because five of the seven things that can land on a hip are guns. The real fix is a per-weapon `carryAngle` on the tool icons, and it is not free: `carryAngle` is added at EVERY slot, so correcting a tool for the hip breaks its pose on the back and the shoulder. Left as it is. A pitchfork on a hip only happens to a class that is not The Hand and already owns three other things.
carry._freshNote: A weapon just taken or just merged announces itself for a couple of seconds: it rides a little higher and draws a little larger. Same signal the ring used, and the reason it existed is unchanged — a seventh thing appearing on a busy character is otherwise easy to miss entirely.
carry._classNote: Each class carries its kit its own way, and it is the cheapest characterisation in the game: no new art, no new stat, one block of numbers. A slot's four facings are the DEFAULT; `byClass` beside them overrides any field of any facing for one class, and only the fields it names -- so `{ "dy": -40 }` raises a shoulder without restating its dx, its depth or its angle. `classSlot` is the other half: it overrides which RESTING slot a weapon asks for, for one class, which is how the Veteran's drum gun goes to his shoulder when weapons.json says every drum gun rides on the back. A `classSlot` entry claims its anchor BEFORE pickup order gets a look in, and it has to: the drum gun and the Varmint Rifle both declare `back`, so whichever was picked up first won it, and the Veteran shouldered his rifle only on the runs where he happened not to own one. Both are resolved into complete anchors ONCE at load, so the merge never runs in the frame loop and the loadout still allocates nothing.
carry._classPickNote: The overrides were chosen to be VISIBLE, and that ruled out the obvious ones. A class's starting weapon is the weapon it fires, so it is in his hands almost every frame of the run and its RESTING slot is the thing you never see: a low hip holster for the scattergun The Kid never holsters would have been a change nobody could photograph. So the two classes whose signature is about the held weapon -- The Kid low at the hip, The Widow braced in on the centreline -- move the `hand` anchor, and the four whose signature is a weapon at rest move the resting one.

byClass._handNote: The Hand's back slot is NOT the pitchfork's private anchor and must not be tuned as if it were. `classSlot` claims it for the fork only on the frames the fork is not the one he just used; six auto-firing weapons hand that slot back and forth all run, so a slung rifle rests here too. It was briefly set to -2.721 -- a quarter turn, to keep the fork standing over his shoulder the way its old 3/4 icon did -- and that stands a RIFLE up like a post, which is the exact pose `_slingNote` records the owner rejecting. Left at -1.15. The carried fork is side-on and points right like the six guns now, so it slings on a back and hangs down a thigh the way they do, at every slot, with no per-weapon `carryAngle` at all: the correction `_twoFamiliesNote` wanted, arrived at by fixing the ART rather than the angles.

back._slingNote: down/up: a long gun on the back is SLUNG -- a diagonal across the torso, muzzle over one shoulder. Facing the camera it is behind him, so the torso hides all but the muzzle, and dx=5 is what pushes that muzzle past the hat brim; centred, 0.9 rad hid the whole gun (measured), and -1.15 stood it up over the shoulder like a post (the owner said so). Side facings keep the steep angle because in profile a sling IS steep.

shoulder._slingNote: down/up: the shoulder slot is the OTHER diagonal of the back sling, so two long guns cross on the back. dx puts the muzzle just outside the hat brim on its own side, which is the only part of a slung gun you see from the front. The Veteran keeps only side-facing overrides now; his front and back are the default cross.

slots._beltNote: The pickaxe and the axe. They are NOT weapons -- they never aim, they never fire, and the two of them would have eaten a third of the six anchors -- so they get two rungs of their own that no weapon can reach: `beltR` and `beltL` are absent from `fallbackOrder`, and nothing in weapons.json names them, so `assignCarrySlots` can never put a gun here. Before this they drew at the player's ORIGIN minus four, which is below his boots, and read as two tools lying on the ground he happened to be standing on. The rung is -12, a new one below the hips at -18, which is the outside of the thigh.

harvest._note: Proximity harvesting. `radius` is how far from the player a node is worked, before the harvestPct stat widens it. Node HP, payouts and the tool ladder live in nodes.json; this is only the reach and the feedback timing.
harvest._dwellNote: Standing on a node ramps its harvest rate. Flat-rate proximity harvesting rewards running — sweeping twenty nodes at base rate beats working one — which inverted the intent and eroded The Hand's stand-your-ground identity in the balance harness. The ramp makes committing to a seam the efficient play.

merge._note: One number, in one place. `world.ts` scales a weapon's damage by this per tier and `offers.ts` prints the resulting before -> after on the merge card, so the card and the sim cannot disagree about what a merge is worth. It used to be a literal 1.6 in world.ts and a hardcoded '+60% damage' in the card text -- two copies of the same balance constant, neither in content, and the card's copy could not even see which weapon it was describing.

offers._note: How the draw is COMPOSED, as opposed to what is in it. docs/UPGRADE_ROSTER.md SS7 is the design; SS8 argues these are draw structure rather than balance and should still live here, which is right -- the rule this project runs on has no exception for numbers that feel structural.
offers._weaponWeightNote: Weapons are weighted up against items so merge pressure survives a big item roster. Once weapon slots are full only OWNED weapons can be offered, so a draw is six weapons against forty items; at 22 items that was six against twenty-two. The roster growing from 22 to 40 therefore cut merge opportunities by about a third without anything being rebalanced, and cleared runs stopped reaching tier 4 at all. 1.6 restored the old weapon share for batch 1. Batch 2 (docs/UPGRADE_ROSTER.md, 48 weapon-upgrade cards) needed it raised again, and by more than SS7.5 predicted: gated cards now fill slot B's OWN quota (see the comment above `if (want > 1)`) instead of falling back to a weapon offer the way an empty gated pool used to, so a weapon now has to outweigh a much bigger field to win the same slot. Measured directly against tests/run.test.ts's hand/kite acceptance ladder (24 seeds, pickSmart) rather than assumed: 1.6 through 4 still failed the >=12/24 bar (4-8 cleared), 6 passed it and every other run.test.ts case (six-class parity, both crossover tests), 8 through 15 were flat or worse — noise at this sample size, not a further trend. Re-measure again if the item or weapon-upgrade count changes.
offers._swapNote: SS7.5's `swap` offer: shop-only, rare, and it prices like a rare item (28-34 elsewhere in items.json) with a premium for the weapon it hands back being an unknown draw rather than a chosen one.
offers._memoryNote: SS7.3. The memory was 90 SECONDS and the shops are 200 seconds apart, so shop suppression was dead by construction -- 100.0% of shop visits reshowed an id from the previous visit. Seconds are the wrong unit anyway: level-ups arrive every ~30s early and every ~90s late, so 90 seconds meant 'the last three boards' at level 5 and 'the last board' at level 30. Boards mean the same thing everywhere. Six is a hard ban, six more at softSuppressWeight.
offers._relaxNote: What a banned card is worth once the filtered pool cannot fill a board. Suppressed rather than banned, for the reason the original code gave and got right: with a thin pool late in a run a hard ban leaves the screen with nothing to show. The escalation order is priority order -- the board memory is surrendered first, the shop's own no-repeat rule last, because that one has a 0% target.
offers._capNote: The three board caps. The first two are SS7.2. maxPerGroup is not: it is what stops 'slot B has no gated card to draw yet, so B, C and D are all behavioural' reproducing the measured 40%-of-boards-are-four-of-a-kind shape in a different colour before batch 2 lands. It is stated in the four buckets tools/offer-stream.ts reports (stat / merge / newWeapon / special) because the SS2 targets are.
offers._tagNote: SS4 and SS7.6. weight *= min(cap, 1 + (per + luck/divisor) * matchingTags). A weight, never a draw: it consumes no RNG and cannot move a seed. At luck 60 the bias is x1.24 per matching tag instead of x1.12, which is a far better luck fantasy than 'slightly more epics' -- a lucky run's cards agree with each other.

_terrainNote: The ground used to be chosen here, one Wang pair for every run. It moved to src/content/maps.json, where each map picks its own ground set, soil set and blight chain. It MOVED rather than being copied: two content files naming the same ground is the same trap as two art groups writing one frame key — the later one silently wins and nothing tells you which is live. The renderer and tools/draw-world.ts both read the world's map now. The reasoning that picked the Home Field's pair is carried over with it: dirt_to_grass_plain over dirt_to_grass and _flat, because the first carried a repeating motif at 32px that read as wallpaper and _flat replaced it with a regular grid weave, subtler but still a repeat. _plain has none, and the argument is not only that — the ground is what two hundred enemies and their bullets are read AGAINST, so a busy floor costs legibility exactly when the screen is fullest. Interest belongs in the props and decals on top of it.
